html:
Figure 1. Brain motor circuits 1

At the bottom of the control hierarchy sit the substrates that actually build and issue motor commands: primary motor cortex (M1), the premotor complex on its anterior bank (PMd/PMv), supplementary and pre-supplementary motor areas (SMA/pre-SMA), and cingulate motor zones (areas in the mid-cingulate sulcus: rostral CMA 2 and caudal CMA 3). These fields are agranular, projection-heavy cortex whose layer-5 pyramidal-tract neurons drive brainstem and spinal circuits. In primates, M1 is distinguished by cortico-motoneuronal synapses onto distal pools, and its neurons carry rich, movement-centric codes: classic cosine tuning for reach direction across the full 360°, speed/velocity signals that scale with peak hand velocity, load/force tuning that predicts compensatory torques under perturbation, and muscle-like synergy weights that linearly reconstruct EMG patterns (e.g., selective post-spike facilitation of FDI vs EDC in forelimb). Many M1 units also encode grasp aperture and wrist pronation/supination during object manipulation, and population activity evolves along low-dimensional manifolds whose rotational components forecast time-varying EMG at millisecond resolution across effectors. Anatomically and computationally, M1 is thus the final common cortical controller: a fast, movement-trajectory generator with direct access to the spinal plant. An anatomical reference traces the corticospinal output pathway (Figure) 4. A textbook-derived map illustrates the motor homunculus along the precentral gyrus (Figure) 5.

Premotor cortex supplies the conditional "if-this-then-act-like-that" scaffolding that shapes those M1 trajectories, with distinct representational niches across its sectors. PMd carries intention and kinematic plans for reaching, including delay-period codes for the chosen target, hand- or eye-centered spatial coordinates, probability distributions over multiple potential targets before commitment, obstacle-aware path biases, and urgency/commit signals that precede movement. PMv (area F5) encodes hand shaping and object-specific grasp synergies-neurons distinguish precision pinch vs power grip, track 3-D object features relevant for affordances, and exhibit mirror responses that map observed goal-directed acts onto the agent’s own motor repertoire. SMA represents internally generated sequence structure, with neurons selective for ordinal position in a sequence, chunk boundaries, and interval timing; pre-SMA emphasizes rule identity, set-switching, and the rapid engagement of a stop/switch policy that interfaces with the hyperdirect pathway. Cingulate motor areas couple skeletomotor plans to value and state, multiplexing action choice with effort cost, expected vigor, and outcome/error feedback while co-modulating autonomic variables (pupil, heart rate) that energize the forthcoming movement. Causally, long-train stimulation across precentral and premotor cortex elicits whole-limb, ethological action fragments (defensive postures, hand-to-mouth, grasp-and-bring), consistent with these regions caching compositional policies; in behavior, their outputs set the initial conditions for the M1 dynamical "engine" and bias which spinal subcircuits will be recruited.

From cortex to muscle, the human motor outflow runs through a handful of well-characterized descending pathways that differ in speed, gain, and the granularity of control. The lateral corticospinal tract (CST)-arising from M1, premotor, and somatosensory cortex-decussates in the pyramids and terminates on spinal interneurons and, in primates, directly on motoneurons innervating intrinsic hand muscles, enabling independent finger forces and fractionated grasp. Parallel corticobulbar fibers target cranial motor nuclei for face, tongue, larynx, and orofacial gestures. Corticoreticular projections descend to the pontomedullary reticular formation and, via reticulospinal tracts, provide fast, large-gain adjustments of posture and multi-joint synergies; in humans, reticulospinal output contributes substantially to proximal arm drive and becomes up-weighted after CST injury, where it supports coarse recovery at the cost of fractionation. Rubrospinal contributions to hand control are modest in humans compared to other mammals but participate in upper-limb kinematics via the dentato-rubro-thalamic loop; vestibulospinal tracts stabilize head/eye/body posture; and tectospinal outputs mediate orienting. Taken together, CST supplies high-bandwidth, fractionated control, while reticulo-/vestibulo-/rubrospinal channels supply posture, gross synergies, start/stop and orienting-an arrangement that lets cortex "write" fine structure on top of robust brainstem controllers. (Riddle et al., 2009; Krimmel et al., 2025; Baker, 2011; Akalu et al., 2023; Rho et al., 2023).

Those brainstem controllers are not passive relays: the mesencephalic locomotor region (cuneiform + pedunculopontine nuclei) forms an executable interface for gait, speed, and posture, with cell-type-specific subcircuits that differentially command locomotor modes and feed ascending state back to basal ganglia and cortex. Superior colliculus stacks rapid visual/multisensory salience with premotor commands for gaze-head redirection, and basal-ganglia output nuclei (GPi/SNr) tonically inhibit these brainstem effectors so that disinhibition selects when an orienting or locomotor program is allowed to run. This subcortical "actuator layer" is therefore both a target of cortical commands and a gate controlled by value-informed loops. (Noga, 2022; Ferreira-Pinto et al., 2021; Ryczko & Dubuc, 2024; Basso & Wurtz, 2011; Fee, 2012; McElvain et al., 2021).

Below the brainstem, spinal circuits transform descending drive into coordinated muscle activity. Identified premotor interneuron classes (e.g., propriospinal relays at C3-C4 for reaching; dorsal interneuron dI3 populations for grasp) route cortical and reticulospinal commands into motoneuron pools while enforcing task-dependent reflex gains via presynaptic inhibition of Ia afferents. Central pattern generators and long propriospinal chains supply rhythmic and multi-segment coordination that descending tracts can start, stop, and shape on the fly. This organization explains why the same cortical pulse can yield context-appropriate motor output: the spinal cord is an adaptive, state-dependent transformer that composes learned synergies under descending and sensory control. (Takei et al., 2010; Isa et al., 2013; Bui et al., 2013; Pierrot-Deseilligny & Burke, 2012).

Critically, low-level motor substrates are not isolated from "control" regions; they are embedded in re-entrant thalamo-cortico-basal ganglia-cerebellar loops that determine when a prepared motor population is allowed to drive effectors, how forcefully, and with what timing. Motor thalamus (VA/VL/VM) is the nexus: it receives powerful excitatory drive from deep cerebellar nuclei and layer-5 motor cortex, modulatory inhibition from GPi/SNr, and projects back to premotor/M1 where it can amplify, time-lock, or redirect population trajectories. Recent anatomy in mice and humans shows overlapping cerebellar and cortical terminals in motor thalamus with BG outputs interdigitated through the same territories-exactly the geometry for rapid thresholding and timing control-while human neurophysiology demonstrates short-latency facilitation of M1 from dentate stimulation (consistent with cerebellar "forward-model" timing). Hyperdirect PFC/pre-SMA input to STN can raise BG output and transiently clamp thalamo-cortical throughput ("global brake"), whereas direct- and indirect-pathway balance tunes movement vigor; in parallel, cerebellar dentato-thalamo-cortical signals set subsecond timing and predictive corrections. In practical terms, PFC decides "what/when," BG sets the gate and gain, cerebellum sets timing/trajectory corrections, and premotor/M1 instantiate the selected plan on the spinal interface. (Koster et al., 2024; Alonso-Martínez et al., 2023; Conner et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Dautan et al., 2021; Basso & Wurtz, 2011).

Putting it together, the motor stack is a layered control fabric. Premotor/SMA/cingulate encode conditional action fragments and internal sequence policy; M1 compresses these into movement-centric population dynamics that directly drive spinal controllers; descending tracts select among brainstem executors with different gains; spinal microcircuits compose synergies and reflex gains to meet the current state; and thalamo-basal-ganglia-cerebellar loops modulate access, vigor, and timing based on goals, conflict, and prediction error.

For robotics, the translation is literal: keep a movement-centric "plant" that runs low-dimensional dynamics to emit torques; front it with a library of action fragments conditioned on context; route outputs through multiple executors with distinct bandwidth/gain (fine vs. gross control); and interpose a centralized gate (BG-like) plus a predictive timing corrector (cerebellum-like) that together decide when the plant is allowed to run and how forcefully it should express the chosen plan.
